title: Acrobats From the Wings
story: A circus troupe builds a human tower: each acrobat can hold up to two others, one per shoulder. It is recorded as a binary tree of the acrobats' numbers. The floor acrobat is the root, and a node's children stand on its shoulders.
The stage manager watches from the right-hand wing and sees only the acrobat nearest that wing on each row. The lighting cue sheet needs exactly those numbers.
task: Write seenFromWing(root). For each level of the tree, take the rightmost node. Return their values starting at the root's level (the floor) and moving up one row at a time.
An empty tree gives an empty list. Trees are shown in level order, like [7, 3, 9, 1, 5], with null marking a missing child. Your function receives real TreeNode objects with val, left and right.
constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep.

examples.explanation: The rows are [7], [3, 9], [1, 5] and [4]. Acrobats 1 and 5 both stand on 3's shoulders, and 9 holds nobody. The rightmost acrobat of each row is 7, 9, 5 and 4. Following right shoulders alone would stop after 7 and 9.
Row 3 holds only acrobat 4, on the far left, but nobody stands to its right, so the manager sees it.

hints: In the first example, the visible acrobat on row 3 stands on the left acrobat of row 2. So what decides visibility: the position under the parent, or the whole row?
Visibility depends only on the row. Given one row in left-to-right order, the answer for it is the last acrobat.
Which traversal hands you the tree one complete row at a time, left to right?
Breadth-first search with a queue. At the start of each level, note the queue's size. Process exactly that many nodes, pushing left child then right child, and record the last value.
bruteForce: The quick guess walks down right shoulders only: root, root.right, root.right.right. It fails when the tower's right side is shorter than its left, as in the first example.

A correct but slow fix walks down from the root again for each row number to collect that row. Up to 500 fresh walks over 1,000 acrobats repeat a lot of work; one level-by-level pass finds every row at once.

walkthrough: The question is about rows, so walk the tree row by row, left to right, and take each row's last node.
• Row [3, 9]. Last is 9. Next row: 3 gives 1 and 5, 9 gives nothing, so [1, 5].
• Row [1, 5]. Last is 5. Next row: only 5 has a child, so [4].
• Row [4]. Last is 4. No children, so stop. Answer [7, 9, 5, 4].

Pushing the left child before the right keeps each row in left-to-right order. If you push the right child first instead, the last node of each row is the leftmost one, which is the view from the other wing.
solution.timeWhy: Every acrobat joins a row once and is looked at once.
solution.spaceWhy: Only the current and next rows are stored, where w is the widest row (up to about n / 2).
solution.takeaway: When the answer depends on a node's level rather than its parent, use breadth-first search, one full level per loop. The first or last node of each level gives the left or right view.
